Measured bundle sizes, the license clause that actually matters, and which of them can drive a canvas or a Three.js scene.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

All three libraries animate the same properties, all three are actively maintained, and all three cost nothing. What separates them is bundle weight, what the license lets you ship, and whether you need something the browser still can’t do by itself.
Start with that last one, because it decides whether you need a library at all. Hovers, enter and exit transitions, single-element keyframes: the platform handles those.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

The table above has the full comparison — sizes, licenses, and which library ships which feature. Save it if you only want the answers.
## The licenses moved, and that’s the story of the last 18 months
Three things changed, and each one invalidated advice you’ll still find in older comparisons.
**GSAP became free — genuinely all of it.** Webflow acquired GreenSock, and [as of version 3.13.0](https://webflow.com/blog/gsap-becomes-free) on 30 April 2025, every plugin that used to sit behind the Club membership ships in the public package: ScrollTrigger, SplitText, MorphSVG, DrawSVG, ScrollSmoother, Draggable, Inertia. Commercial use included, no fee.
It is not, however, an open source license. The [standard license](https://gsap.com/community/standard-license/) is a custom “no charge” grant with one real exclusion: you can’t use GSAP to build a no-code tool that lets users create animations in competition with Webflow. For a product team shipping a website or an app, that clause never fires. If you’re building a design tool, read it before you commit.
**Framer Motion became Motion.** The package is now `motion`, MIT licensed, and `framer-motion` is kept alive as a re-export — both published 12.42.2 within seconds of each other. The library itself stays free; a separate [Motion+](https://motion.dev/plus) tier (£299 one-time for the personal plan) sells premium components, examples and a visual editor on top.
**Anime.js v4 is a different library than v3.** The [rewrite landed](https://github.com/juliangarnier/anime/releases/tag/v4.0.0) on 3 April 2025. The global `anime` object is gone, replaced by named ESM exports — `animate`, `createTimeline`, `createDraggable`, `onScroll`, `stagger`, `utils`, `waapi`. Still MIT. Your v3 code will not run against it, and the port is manual.
## What each one actually costs
Published bundle-size figures measure the vendor’s own best case, so I bundled the smallest working import for each library with esbuild 0.25.0, minified, and gzipped the result — GSAP 3.15.0, Motion 12.42.2, Anime.js 4.5.0.
- **3.4 kB** — `motion/mini`, driving the Web Animations API directly. No independent transforms, no SVG paths, no sequences.
- **5.1 kB** — Anime.js’s `waapi` module. Same trade.
- **13.2 kB** — Anime.js `animate()`. With a timeline and scroll observer, 19.1 kB.
- **24.7 kB** — Motion’s hybrid `animate()`. Springs, layout animations, independent transforms.
- **28.2 kB** — GSAP core. With ScrollTrigger, 46.1 kB.
- **43.9 kB** — `motion/react`, for a single `<motion.div>`.
The React bindings are the most expensive entry point here, which is worth knowing before you reach for one.
## The APIs differ more than the capabilities
Take one staggered fade — three cards, 24px up, 600ms, 80ms apart. GSAP writes it as a single `gsap.from()` with a `stagger` value, inferring the starting state and reading durations in seconds. Motion splits the call into two objects, what changes and then how it changes, with `stagger()` supplying the delay. Anime.js puts both in one object and counts in milliseconds.
Written natively, you loop the elements yourself and multiply the index by 80 to get each offset. At this size, that loop is the entire difference — which is the honest case for shipping nothing.
## GSAP: pick it for sequencing and SVG
GSAP earns its 28 kB when an animation has structure — a timeline with labels, nested tweens, relative offsets, and something driving playback from scroll position. Nothing else here matches ScrollTrigger’s pinning and scrub behavior, and MorphSVG has no real equivalent in the other two.
It’s also the only one of the three with a first-party React integration that solves cleanup properly: [`@gsap/react`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@gsap/react) and its `useGSAP()` hook, at roughly 1.1M downloads a week. That combination bundles to 31.1 kB — still 13 kB under Motion’s React entry point.
The trade-off is release cadence. GSAP shipped 3.13.0 in April 2025, 3.14.0 in December, and 3.15.0 in April 2026 — three minor releases in a year, against Motion’s near-weekly patches. For a mature engine that’s a reasonable pace, not a warning sign.
## Motion: pick it for component-driven UI
Motion is the only one of the three built around a component model rather than a call to `animate()`. If your animations are tied to React or Vue state — a modal that mounts, a list that reorders — `motion/react` does layout animations and gesture handling you would otherwise write by hand.
Its hybrid engine is the interesting architectural bet: hand animations to the browser’s native compositor where possible, fall back to JavaScript where the Web Animations API can’t express what you asked for. That’s why the mini and full builds differ by 21 kB.
Weekly downloads say where it lives: `motion` at 16.3M and `framer-motion` at 40.9M, against GSAP’s 4.0M and Anime.js’s 1.0M (18–24 July 2026). Transitive React dependencies inflate those totals, but they tell you which library your bundle probably already contains.
## Anime.js: pick it when you want the engine, not the framework
Anime.js v4 is the cheapest way to get real animation features without adopting a framework’s model. 13.2 kB buys you timelines, SVG morphing and draw-on, a physics-based draggable, a scroll observer, and text splitting. GSAP charges roughly 15 kB more for the same category of features; Motion has no SVG morphing at all, and puts text splitting behind Motion+.
What you give up: there is no official React or Vue binding, so lifecycle and cleanup are your problem. And because v4 is a rewrite, much of the tutorial material you’ll find still targets the v3 API. Check that any example you copy uses named imports.
## Canvas, WebGL and Three.js
All three animate a Three.js scene, for a duller reason than you’d expect: `mesh.position.x` is an ordinary number on an ordinary object. Any library that tweens object properties can drive a 3D scene, and all three do — including nested objects, which is the case that matters.
I checked this against Three.js 0.185.1 rather than trusting the docs. Pointing `gsap.to()` or Anime.js’s `animate()` at `mesh.position`, `mesh.rotation` or `mesh.material.opacity` lands every value exactly — no adapter, no plugin, no wrapper.
**`motion/mini` is the trap.** The 3.4 kB build that makes Motion look cheapest cannot animate JavaScript objects, and it does not tell you so — pass it an object and it throws no error, logs nothing, and leaves the value untouched. You need the full 24.7 kB `motion` build for anything that isn’t a DOM or SVG element.
What actually separates them here is narrower than the size table suggests:
- **GSAP is the only one with canvas-library plugins.** PixiPlugin and EaselPlugin ship in the free package. [PixiPlugin](https://gsap.com/docs/v3/Plugins/PixiPlugin/) takes rotation in degrees instead of radians, accepts CSS colour strings instead of `0xFF0000`, and exposes `blur`, `saturation` and `hue` without you constructing filter instances. Motion and Anime.js have no equivalent.
- **All three expose a frame loop you can hang a renderer off**: `gsap.ticker`, Motion’s `frame`, Anime.js’s `engine` and `createTimer()`. One clock for DOM and canvas means your tweens and your render calls can’t drift apart, and pausing the page pauses both.
- **The platform is out entirely.** `element.animate()` takes an element. There is no native path to a canvas or a WebGL uniform; you write `requestAnimationFrame` and interpolate by hand.
If your page is a DOM interface *and* a canvas, one library covering both is a real saving — which points at GSAP or Anime.js, since Motion’s cheap build is the one that can’t cross over.
Neither is the default inside Three.js codebases, though. [`@tweenjs/tween.js`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@tweenjs/tween.js) sits at 8.6M downloads a week against Three.js’s own 13.2M, and [`@react-spring/three`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@react-spring/three) at 2.0M covers React Three Fiber — which none of these three integrates with first-party. Reach for GSAP or Anime.js when the same logic also drives your DOM; if the project is 3D end to end, the Three.js-native tools are better trodden.
## When to ship none of them
The Web Animations API has been [Baseline widely available since September 2020](https://webstatus.dev/features/web-animations). `element.animate()` gives you keyframes, easing, playback control, and promises, at zero bytes. For most enter/exit and hover work, a library is 25 kB spent on ergonomics.
Two gaps keep the libraries relevant:
**Scroll-driven animations are still not Baseline.** Chrome shipped `animation-timeline` in 115 (July 2023) and Safari followed in 26 (September 2025), but [Firefox has no release yet](https://webstatus.dev/features/scroll-driven-animations). If scroll-linked motion matters to your product, ScrollTrigger or `onScroll()` is a polyfill you don’t have to write.
**There is no native timeline.** Sequencing more than two or three elements with `element.animate()` means managing delays by hand, and changing one duration upstream means recomputing all of them. That’s where a 13 kB timeline pays for itself.
View transitions, meanwhile, [reached Baseline on 14 October 2025](https://webstatus.dev/features/view-transitions) when Firefox 144 shipped — page and route transitions are now a platform feature, not a library one.
## The decision, in one pass
Work down the list and stop at the first match.
1. No scroll linking, multi-step timeline, SVG morphing or canvas? Use the platform.
2. Component-driven UI in React or Vue, with layout and gesture animation? Motion.
3. Timelines, SVG and canvas at the lowest weight, framework-independent? Anime.js.
4. The animation *is* the product — scroll narratives, pinned sections, morphing artwork, a WebGL scene sharing a clock with the DOM? GSAP, and budget the 46 kB.
The one thing worth re-checking before you commit is the GSAP license clause, and only if what you’re building lets other people author animations.
